canonical_question: Is the wear rate of 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ mm³/N m at 300 °C actually lower or higher than the 6.4 × 10⁻⁶ mm³/N m at RT, and why does the text not explicitly state the magnitude difference?

question_variants.question: Is the wear rate of 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ mm³/N m at 300 °C actually lower or higher than the 6.4 × 10⁻⁶ mm³/N m at RT, and why does the text not explicitly state the magnitude difference?
question_variants.resolution_summary: The wear rate at 300 °C (2.5 × 10⁻⁵ mm³/N m) is higher than at RT (6.4 × 10⁻⁶ mm³/N m). The text lists them in order of temperature (RT then 300 °C) but the values are not explicitly compared in magnitude in the sentence, requiring numerical interpretation.

answers.answer: The wear rate at 300 °C (2.5 × 10⁻⁵ mm³/N m) is approximately 4 times higher than the wear rate at RT (6.4 × 10⁻⁶ mm³/N m). The text states: 'low average wear rates of 6.4 × 10 –6 and 2.5 × 10 –5 mm 3 /N m at RT and 300 °C, respectively.'
answers.conditions: RT and 300 °C, sliding against alloy steel
answers.measurement_outcome: Wear rate RT: 6.4e-6, Wear rate 300C: 2.5e-5 mm^3/N m
evidence_spans: In this work, a refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film of equimolar CuMoTaWV was deposited on silicon and 304 stainless-steel substrates using DC-magnetron sputtering.
A sputtering target was developed by partial sintering of an equimolar powder mixture of Cu, Mo, Ta, W, and V using spark plasma sintering.
The target was used to sputter a nanocrystalline RHEA film with a thickness of ∼900 nm and an average grain size of 18 nm.
